newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl firm on strict EMU, Bonn focuses on '99.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl firm on strict EMU, Bonn focuses on '99.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl rushed to the vanguard of Germany's EMU hardliners on Tuesday, pledging Bonn would meet the 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP goal on time and chiding critics who would delay the single currency.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel chimed in, saying Bonn was working tirelessly to meet the criteria, while one of his aides hinted Germany would convert its outstanding federal debt to euros once the new currency was launched on January 1, 1999.

The chairman of Germany's largest bank, Rolf Breuer of Deutsche Bank AG, dismissed talk of delaying economic and monetary union (EMU) and chided politicians for quibbling over whether the deficit target was 3.0 percent exactly or could be flexible.

All this almost drowned out a dogged EMU delay campaign by Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, whose open challenge to Kohl to sketch out his position clearly prompted the chancellor to promise Bonn would meet the 3.0 percent goal.

Kohl, who normally avoids precise statements about the Maastricht target, apparently opted for a clearer stand in a tactical move to blunt Stoiber's campaign and signal to France it could not massively overshoot the deficit criterion.
But Stoiber, whose super-stable euro campaign seems mostly driven by the byzantine demands of Bavarian politics, crowned his discretion with a veiled threat of further debate.
"We're staying with 3.0 -- that's no problem -- and with the schedule," Kohl told about 1,500 entrepreneurs at the 50th anniversary of the Bavarian employers' association.

Recalling that parliament demanded a strict interpretation of the criteria when it ratified the Maastrict treaty, he added in a jab at the Bavarian premier sitting in the front row: "That stands, it is binding, there is no use discussing it anymore.
In a confusing twist of the "decimal point debate," Waigel avoided spelling out the deficit goal as "three-point-zero" and hinted convergence was more important than the 1999 deadline.
Analysts believe Kohl wants the euro launched in 1999 even if the Maastricht criteria are watered down to achieve this.

But Stoiber's Eurosceptical campaign, designed to keep rival parties from stealing votes from the ruling Christian Social Union (CSU) in a state election late next year, has forced Kohl to make pledges analysts doubt he can keep.

"This was a purely political manoeuvre by Kohl to keep the euro on track," said Bernd Kruth at Westdeutsche Landesbank in Duesseldorf. "Someday, Kohl is going to end up saying 'sorry, we didn't reach the 3.0 percent target'."

The tougher line could also be Kohl's signal to France, which has already said it would miss the 3.0 percent target, that Germany would not tolerate a massive budget overshoot from any country wanting to join EMU in the first wave.
"This indicates Germany does not want to give up," one source close to the Bundesbank told Reuters in Frankfurt.

In another EMU-related move, Finance Ministry State Secretary Juergen Stark said he would urge Waigel that all tradeable federal debt -- about half the 900 billion mark total -- be converted to euros in 1999.
This would ensure the German debt market, the world's third largest, would not lose its pre-eminent role when EMU comes.

Deutsche Bank's Breuer tried to take some distance from the heated EMU debate of recent days by stressing the decision which countries would join in 1999 "will not depend on mathematics...but the trend" and criticised talk of a delay.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker criticised the criteria debate in Germany and said it highlighted a growing rift between Kohl's Christian democrats (CDU) and Stoiber's CSU that was damaging for the project.
"I find this German discussion unhealthy," he told MDR radio on the day his country took over the rotating European Union presidency.
Stoiber's anti-Euro campaign has become so shrill in recent days that the German media turned out in force to witness his first meeting with Kohl since the debate broke out.

Kohl, whose body language speaks volumes, strode into Munich's Philharmonic Hall, quickly shook hands with Stoiber and then promptly turned away. The assembled business men and women broke out into loud laughter at the scene.
